## Problem
Calling my dot, BlueDot, rings without connecting to a usable voice conversation. This standalone report separates the cross-device dot-call failure from the Windows startup/process and New Chat defects in #49877.

## Reproduction
1. Open the existing dot conversation.
2. Select the phone/call button.
3. Wait for the call to connect.

Actual: repeated ringing without an answer or voice connection. Another affected user reports ringing followed by “Call failed”.
Expected: a usable two-way voice conversation, or a bounded timeout with an actionable error and retry path.

## Confirmed observations and corroboration
- My original report reproduced the failure in the iPhone app and Windows web interface: #49877.
- [1 October update](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/49877#issuecomment-5930710381): the same unanswered ringing also reproduced from my MacBook.
- [marcusglee11](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/49877#issuecomment-5943583592) independently reported unanswered dot calls on 2 October, explicitly without confirming the startup or New Chat symptoms.
- [Yeoj5190](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/49877#issuecomment-5943845191) reported ringing followed by “Call failed” on both Mac and iPhone despite reinstalling the apps; normal ChatGPT voice still worked for that user.
- [My 2 October follow-up](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/49877#issuecomment-5947935497) confirmed another failed phone call. I did not retest PC or Mac in that follow-up.

Exact Mac/iPhone client builds and call diagnostics have not been captured. The Windows desktop version recorded in the original mixed report was 26.928.3736.0; that is not a verified version for the web or mobile call clients.

## Scope and related reports
No root cause is established. The Windows startup logs in #49877 do not establish the cause of this call failure. Its suggested duplicates (#49376, #49506, #48896, #49447) concern startup/New Chat rather than this cross-device call symptom.

Older related report #49499 describes dot calls failing within seconds across desktop, web and iOS, with a recorded WebRTC media error. A shared cause with our unanswered-ringing reports is unconfirmed; please consolidate if appropriate.

A fresh repository search on 4 October found no newer dedicated report matching this unanswered-call symptom. Please investigate dot-call connection handling separately from Windows startup and New Chat, and advise which sanitised call diagnostics would help.

items.body:
## Summary

On Windows with Codex desktop 26.930.31730 (build 12947), an official Chrome extension-controlled tab initially renders Baidu Talent, then the same top-level tab becomes `about:blank`. The user reports that a fresh ordinary tab in the same Chrome window/profile remains usable. Updating the desktop app did not resolve the controlled-path reproduction.

This is a Windows/Baidu-specific corroboration of the route-dependent symptom in #35700, not a claim that its exact root cause has been established.

## Environment

- OS: Windows (exact OS build not collected)
- Codex desktop: 26.930.31730, build 12947, production release channel
- Browser: existing Google Chrome profile with the official connected extension; exact Chrome/extension versions not collected
- Tested: 2026-10-04

## Minimal observed reproduction

1. Through the supported Chrome browser-control API, create a fresh tab at `https://talent.baidu.com/`.
2. The initial response shows a nonempty recruitment page at `https://talent.baidu.com/jobs/social`, including navigation, search and login controls.
3. After intervening read-only checks and a 10-second wait, inspect the same tab's URL/title and screenshot.
4. URL and title are now `about:blank`; the screenshot is empty.

The 10-second wait is an observation interval, not a measured exact transition time. No login, form submission or injected page modification was performed in this reproduction.

## Control

The user opened the same official URL manually in a fresh ordinary tab in the same Chrome window/profile and confirmed that it displayed normally after the requested wait. That control tab was intentionally not claimed by the automation session.

Other websites remain controllable. BOSS resume navigation and Liepin candidate-site navigation also showed similar top-level blank/redirect symptoms, but this report does not assume they have the same root cause.

## Expected and actual

Expected: the successfully rendered controlled top-level page stays usable, or navigation returns a clear actionable failure.

Actual: transient success followed by an unexplained top-level `about:blank` state. Captured error/warning logs did not explain the transition.

## What remains unknown

Current production website assets now identify an active site-owned blank-navigation mechanism on Baidu and an auto-initializing enforcement asset on Liepin (see source findings below). The exact checker fired during CUA attachment, the initiating runtime stack, and the separate session inventory hang remain unobserved. BOSS attribution is still unknown. This is not classified as a CAPTCHA or a lost-login issue.

## Requested guidance

Please provide a supported diagnostic method to distinguish site-triggered navigation from client/extension tab cleanup, and advise whether there is a supported non-debugger fallback for normal visible Chrome interaction. No browser security settings, credentials or cookies were changed.

## Privacy

This report intentionally excludes account identities, local paths, tab identifiers, screenshots containing personal data and raw logs. A redacted event summary is available; no private workspace or browser storage is attached.

## Follow-up verification (2026-10-05)

- Codex in-app browser: a fresh direct navigation to the already-observed final Baidu route initially rendered, then URL/title became top-level `about:blank`. This did not depend solely on the Chrome-extension backend.
- Later Chrome tab enumeration timed out and the browser JavaScript session reset automatically. Fresh inventory initialization subsequently timed out at both 30-second and 60-second execution limits. These initialization failures are recorded separately from the earlier blank transition.
- Supported Windows native `@oai/sky` fallback: with the actual visible Chrome window selected, normal address-bar navigation retained the existing Baidu login, reached personal center and the resume creation form, and successfully switched resume type. Native BOSS navigation reached its visible onboarding form. No user details were entered and no form was saved or submitted.
- Native fallback is intermittent: a later fresh-tab operation/state check ended with the tool's current-URL confidence safety stop. One secondary-window capture also returned AX and pixels from different visible pages; switching to the actual visible main window aligned them. No enforcement was bypassed.
- Local prerequisite checks found no existing proxy variables or system proxy, no stale CLI override, and enabled browser/computer-use plugins. Shell connectivity checks alone do not establish helper connectivity.

These observations establish a usable native alternative for the verified steps, not a permanent repair or an exact root cause. No raw logs, screenshots, identities, local paths or browser storage are attached.

## Additional controlled comparison (2026-10-05)

- Liepin through supported Windows native UI reached its basic onboarding form, switched the student option, and remained nonblank after a normal reload. No personal details were entered or saved.
- A fresh independent helper session completed `cua.getState()` in 1.4383 seconds. The original session still timed out at 30 seconds. These results narrow the inventory hang to session state without establishing its cause.
- The working independent session created a fresh Baidu `/jobs/social` Chrome tab: initial recruitment content was visible; after approximately 10 seconds the same top-level URL/title became `about:blank`, with empty accessibility content and screenshot. The observation returned in about 1.15 seconds, so this was not an inventory timeout.
- An existing empty Baidu `/jobs/resume/create` test tab created through native UI was then attached/read through CUA. It initially showed the full internship form; approximately 10 seconds later the same tab became top-level `about:blank`. No navigation, clicking, typing or saving occurred during that comparison. This rules out a defect limited to CUA's fresh-tab creation route, but does not distinguish a site response to attachment from client target lifecycle behavior.
- Launcher/runtime paths exist in the current configuration. Multiple helper groups share the app parent; none were terminated because current-chat ownership was not uniquely identifiable.

No private IDs, account identities, local paths, raw logs or screenshots are included. The issue remains unresolved; native UI is a verified operational alternative for the specific steps, not a permanent browser-control repair.

## Primary public-source findings (2026-10-05)

Read-only analysis used anonymously accessible production HTML and scripts; no fetched script was executed, no browser cookies were exported, and no detection bypass was used.

- Baidu production HTML at https://talent.baidu.com/jobs/social references [Page.695b8d85.chunk.js](https://talent-offical-static-prod.cdn.bcebos.com/hcm-recruitment/talent-offical-static-prod/client/static/js/Page.695b8d85.chunk.js) and [vendor.e58a1081.chunk.js](https://talent-offical-static-prod.cdn.bcebos.com/hcm-recruitment/talent-offical-static-prod/client/static/js/vendor.e58a1081.chunk.js). The active root component installs a debugging-detector listener and launches it on mount for an ordinary URL. When its listener receives a truthy result, the Page asset assigns the page location to `about:blank`. The redirect/listener is at zero-based UTF-16 offset 14505 on line 1 of the current Page asset.
- The vendor detector has a 500-ms inter-loop default delay and formatting/timing-related checkers. No fixed 10-second redirect timer was found in this identified path. The observed 10-second intervals are observation intervals. The exact CUA-triggered checker remains unknown; static code plus native-versus-attachment comparison strongly supports a site response but is not a runtime trace.
- The unauthenticated public shell at https://c.liepin.com/resume/create and its public homepage both reference [security/1.0.0/security.min.js](https://concat.lietou-static.com/fe-lib-pc/v6/security/1.0.0/security.min.js). It auto-initializes a guard enabled by default, has console/devtools-related probes, and can replace the page location with its default `about:blank` destination, with DOM clearing as a fallback. Static initialization is verified; the specific probe during CUA control was not captured.
- A bounded literal search of BOSS public homepage HTML and two relevant public assets did not identify the same redirect path. This negative result does not rule out other, encoded, dynamic or authenticated code. No common cause across all three sites is asserted.

## Continuous supported-native route acceptance (2026-10-05)

Using one dedicated empty test tab in the existing Chrome profile, without CUA attachment:

- Baidu: personal-center/create-form roundtrip; internship option and city dropdown; normal reload.
- BOSS: official resume link to basic onboarding; student option; normal reload; homepage return and resume reopening.
- Liepin: official homepage redirect; manual basic form; student option and status dropdown; normal reload and form reopening.
- Cross-site return Baidu → BOSS → Liepin → Baidu: full form and internship selection remained visible after an additional 20-second observation.

All these page-operation checks passed without a top-level blank transition or URL-confidence stop in this run. This goes beyond initial rendering, but covers only the initial forms: full profile saving, all six BOSS steps, and applications were not tested. Earlier native URL-confidence stops remain a separate limitation. The affected workflows now use this supported native route locally; the original browser-control incompatibility and session hang remain open. No security settings, vendor code, credentials, cookies, or global model settings were changed. No identities, private screenshots, local paths, raw logs or browser storage are attached.

### Observed problem

One older completed turn in an existing user-facing conversation has no projected items, although its original rollout records survive. Other history is readable, so this is not a report that every turn or every conversation is empty.

A targeted desktop-provided read earlier on 2026-10-04 returned the target turn as completed with an empty items array. A preserved October 2 analysis snapshot contains the turn but no corresponding projected thread items; its first-user/last-assistant anchors are empty. These are dated observations, not a claim that the current entire live database has been audited or that native UI completeness has been verified.

### Preserved source observations

The exact bounded source slice contains 215 original JSONL records and was preserved byte-for-byte locally. It includes matching task start/end boundaries, one legacy user_message event and eleven legacy agent_message events, but no item_completed event. Saved response items, paired tool calls/results and citation information are also present. A nearby normally projected turn contains item_completed events.

This suggests a possible legacy-event materialization gap, but the absence of item_completed is only a hypothesis about the cause, not a confirmed diagnosis. items.body:
### What issue are you seeing?

This is a regression in an existing Codex CLI workflow.

For a long time I have used two valid ChatGPT/Codex accounts and switched between them when one account reached its rate limit. I do **not** need hot-swapping inside a currently running turn/process.

The workflow was:

```bash
# CODEX_HOME is ~/codex in my setup

cd ~/codex/
cp auth.json.1 auth.json

cd ~/repo/
codex --yolo

# work until account 1 reaches its rate limit, then exit Codex

cd ~/codex/
cp auth.json auth.json.1
cp auth.json.2 auth.json

cd ~/repo/
codex --yolo resume
```

Historically, the new Codex invocation loaded account 2 from `auth.json` and resumed the same conversation/thread. This allowed me to continue the same coding session with the other account.

That no longer works. After replacing `auth.json` and starting a new `codex ... resume` invocation, Codex continues to use the previous account / stale authentication state instead of the account stored in the current auth file.

Both auth files are valid. The second account's auth was confirmed working shortly before reproducing this.

### Why this is a regression rather than a multi-account feature request

I am **not** asking for first-class auth profiles (#4432), and I am **not** asking a running app-server to silently hot-reload credentials mid-turn (#43010 / #42771).

I am exiting the CLI and starting a **new CLI invocation** with `resume`.

Before the managed/persistent app-server behavior, that invocation picked up the currently selected persisted credentials and could resume the existing thread under the other account.

The persistent app-server now appears to survive the CLI lifecycle and keep the old account alive across what, from the user's perspective, is a new Codex launch. That breaks a previously working workflow.

The explanation in #42771 says that `auth.json` is a credential cache used for subsequent app-server launches. The problem here is that ordinary CLI exit/relaunch/resume no longer creates the auth boundary that previously existed, so the "subsequent launch" keeps inheriting stale auth state.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Have two valid ChatGPT accounts usable with Codex CLI.
2. Save valid auth state for each account as `auth.json.1` and `auth.json.2`.
3. Copy account 1 into the active auth file.
4. Start Codex in a repository and create/use a thread:

   ```bash
   codex --yolo
   ```

5. Exit Codex.
6. Save the latest account-1 auth state, then copy account 2 into the active auth file:

   ```bash
   cp auth.json auth.json.1
   cp auth.json.2 auth.json
   ```

7. Resume the same thread:

   ```bash
   codex --yolo resume
   ```

8. Check the active account / usage state.

### Expected behavior

A **new Codex CLI invocation** should use the currently selected persisted credentials and allow the existing local thread to be resumed with that account, as it did previously.

At minimum, there needs to be a supported account-switch boundary that:

- does not destroy local session/thread state,
- does not require creating a separate `CODEX_HOME` per account (which separates session state),
- and allows `codex resume` to continue the same thread after changing accounts.

### Actual behavior

The resumed CLI remains attached to the old account/auth state even though the active auth file has been replaced with valid credentials for account 2.

Restarting the managed app-server is not an acceptable substitute if it logs the user out or otherwise invalidates the currently selected auth state.

### User impact

This workflow matters specifically when one paid account reaches its Codex rate limit during a long coding session and I want to continue the **same thread** with another account I already pay for.

I do not want to buy a more expensive subscription or additional credits merely to compensate for a CLI regression that removed a previously working account-switching workflow.

If there is no supported way to retain this workflow, it materially reduces the value of my Codex subscription(s), to the point that I would cancel rather than upgrade or buy credits.

### Environment

- Platform: Linux
- Date reproduced: 2026-10-04
- Codex CLI version: `codex-cli 0.160.0`
- Auth mode: ChatGPT account auth
- Session flow: local CLI/TUI, `resume`

items.body:
### What version of Codex CLI is running?

codex-mcp-client 0.155 to 0.160, as seen in our server logs. We operate the MCP server, not the client.

### What subscription do you have?

Not applicable (observed server-side across users)

### Which model were you using?

Not applicable

### What platform is your computer?

Unknown (observed server-side)

### Codex doctor report

not available

### What issue are you seeing?

We run Oddlynew's remote MCP server at https://mcp.oddlynew.com/mcp (Streamable HTTP, OAuth). Codex negotiates protocol 2025-06-18 and sends its POSTs with a bearer token. Its `GET /mcp` (the request that opens the SSE stream) never carries an `Authorization` header in our logs, so our server answers 401 with `WWW-Authenticate`.

In the 7 days to 2026-10-04 we saw 4,640 of these GETs, about 660 a day. None had an `Authorization` header, and they carried `MCP-Protocol-Version: 2024-11-05` rather than the negotiated version. In a full-fidelity sample of the same week, 72% were followed within 10 seconds by a successful request from the same IP address and user agent, so the 401 does not appear to break sessions.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Add an OAuth-protected Streamable HTTP MCP server and sign in.
2. Keep a Codex session connected to the server.
3. In the server log: repeated `GET /mcp` with no `Authorization`, answered 401.

### What is the expected behavior?

The 2025-06-18 authorization spec says authorization "MUST be included in every HTTP request from client to server, even if they are part of the same logical session", and uses `GET /mcp` as its example. The GET should carry the bearer, or be skipped if Codex does not use the stream.

### Additional information

Our server will answer this GET with 405 soon (we are fixing our side), so for us the remaining cost is one wasted request each time.

## Problem

The agent can enumerate browser surfaces but cannot open a public documentation page in the advertised in-app browser. Browser access fails because the security gate cannot verify the admin-enforced policy. A later attempt to open the OpenAI developer documentation homepage times out and resets the computer-use kernel.

## Steps and observed results

1. Call `await cua.getState()`.
2. Browser inventory advertises `Codex In-app Browser` with type `iab` and an empty tab list; it also advertises `Codex MCP Apps`. Native app inventory includes Safari. Chrome is not available through this session's browser provider.
3. Call `await cua.createBrowserTab("iab", "https://www.waveshare.com/wiki/2.9inch_e-Paper_Module_Manual", {visible: true})` for a user-authorized, read-only documentation task.
4. The call returns the following error before granting page access:

```text
Browser Use could not complete this action because a browser security check was unavailable. Reason: The admin-enforced policy could not be verified, so access was not granted. Browser use could not verify the admin-enforced policy before accessing https://www.waveshare.com. This failure may be temporary. The agent may retry after the issue is resolved, but must not bypass browser security controls or use an indirect workaround.
```

5. After the user explicitly requests a browser retest and a bug report, `cua.getState()` still advertises the in-app browser.
6. Call `await cua.createBrowserTab("iab", "https://developers.openai.com", {visible: true})`.
7. After approximately 30 seconds, the tool returns:

```text
js execution timed out; kernel reset, rerun your request
```

The second result is a timeout, not proof that OpenAI's domain was denied. No security bypass was attempted.

## Expected behavior

The advertised browser should either complete the applicable policy verification and open an authorized read-only page, or report an actionable policy failure with its source and supported recovery steps. A failed policy check should not leave browser creation hanging until the tool resets its kernel.

The agent cannot use the in-app browser to inspect public vendor documentation. Native-app inventory/control was available earlier in the session, so this is a browser-access failure rather than evidence that all computer-use functionality is unavailable.

### What version of the Codex App are you using?

- Linux desktop package metadata: `26.928.31416`.
- The active desktop client identifies itself in recent host logs as `26.930.31730`; both observations are provided because the package and active client version strings differ.

### What subscription do you have?

Not included in this report; the failure occurs during project-trust verification.

### What platform is your computer?

`uname -mprs`: `Linux 7.2.5-3-omarchy x86_64 unknown`

Client: ChatGPT Android Remote; host: Linux desktop app.

### What issue are you seeing?

Starting a new Codex Remote chat from Android for an existing saved Linux desktop project fails with a project-trust error. Sending messages to existing chats on the same host works.

The saved desktop project uses a path containing a symlink, while the mobile error names the resolved physical path. They are the same workspace directory, not separate copies. The desktop has one saved project for this workspace.

Paths and project names are sanitized throughout this report:

```text
/home/<user>/projects -> /data/projects
saved desktop project: /home/<user>/projects/<workspace>
resolved realpath:     /data/projects/<workspace>
mobile error path:     /data/projects/<workspace>
```

The mobile screenshot shows the selected project and connected host, a short initial prompt (`Test`), and:

```text
The last remote turn failed.

Can't verify project trust for /data/projects/<workspace>. Open the repository in Codex on the remote computer and make a trust choice, then select that repository's original directory and try again. You can also start in Read only mode. If this continues, update Codex on the remote computer.
```

The user-level config already contains an explicit trust decision for the saved path:

```toml
[projects."/home/<user>/projects/<workspace>"]
trust_level = "trusted"
```

There is no explicit entry for `/data/projects/<workspace>`. Both spellings resolve to that same physical directory. This saved workspace folder is not itself a Git repository; it contains repositories.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Observed workflow:

1. On a Linux desktop host, use a workspace beneath a symlinked parent directory, as in the layout above.
2. Save the workspace in the desktop app using its logical `/home/...` path, and establish an explicit trusted decision for that path.
3. Connect to that host using Android Codex Remote.
4. Select the existing saved project and start a new chat with a short prompt.
5. Observe the trust-verification failure naming the resolved `/data/...` path.
6. Sending messages to already available chats still works.

The saved project path, trust entry and realpath equivalence were checked locally. The failure and existing-chat behavior are the user's live observations. No independent minimal public-workspace reproduction or controlled trust-entry experiment has been run yet. No trust settings were modified during diagnosis.

### What is the expected behavior?

A saved project accessed through a symlink and its resolved path should have consistent project identity and trust lookup. An existing explicit trust decision should be evaluated against the correct project identity, with explicit untrusted decisions and other security boundaries preserved.

The same project should not require a second project entry or a second trust decision solely because Remote startup chooses another spelling of the same path.

### Additional information

**Suspected cause, not confirmed:** inconsistent symlink/canonical-path handling between desktop project storage, mobile startup and project-trust verification. Local desktop inspection found that workspace-root metadata includes a realpath mapping, while the desktop folder-trust confirmation code looks up the saved path in `config.projects`. This is supporting context, not proof of the exact failing mobile code path.

The precise failing RPC and mobile implementation have not been identified. The new chat's execution mode was not recorded. The displayed error names the original workspace directory, rather than a generated managed-worktree destination.

Related reports:
- #30808: symlink versus canonical-path project matching and hidden remote chats. This report concerns failure to start a new mobile chat, with existing chats still usable.
- #43239: Android Remote project-trust failure for newly generated linked worktrees. The error text overlaps, but the path in this report is the existing saved workspace, not a generated worktree.

Please consolidate if these share an underlying defect. Company names, usernames, host identifiers, session identifiers, credentials, raw logs and conversation history are omitted. The screenshot's relevant error is transcribed above instead of publishing the original image.

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

App (ChatGPT desktop app for Linux, 26.924.22138, CachyOS package `chatgpt-desktop-bin`, GNOME 50.5 on Wayland)

### What feature would you like to see?

Global dictation on Linux: press a shortcut in any app, speak, and have the transcript inserted into the focused field, as on macOS and Windows.

The Linux build ships the shared global dictation code, but the main-process bundle (`.vite/build/main-*.js` in `app.asar`) excludes Linux in three places. Minified names are from 26.924.22138; 26.915.31945 excludes Linux in the same three places. The renderer's `dictation.global` capability, rollout and access checks apply on top of this; I can't tell how they evaluate for Linux accounts.

1. **Platform check.** This predicate excludes Linux even when the renderer capability is enabled. It's used by `applyLifecycleOrThrow()`, `getHotkeyState()` and the hotkey setters:
   ```js
   function …(){return process.platform===`darwin`||process.platform===`win32`}
   ```
2. **No Linux key-release detection.** Hold-to-talk and double-press-to-start both depend on release events. macOS uses the native `bare-modifier-monitor` helper; Windows uses a native `KeyboardMonitor` in 26.924.22138 (a PowerShell watcher in 26.915.31945). The `linux` case throws `Global dictation hotkey release watching is not supported.`
3. **No Linux paste.** macOS first invokes the focused app's Paste menu command through Accessibility and falls back to `osascript` (`keystroke "v" using command down`); Windows runs `[System.Windows.Forms.SendKeys]::SendWait('^v')` through PowerShell. The `linux` case throws `Global dictation paste is not supported on this OS.`

Shortcut registration would also need work on Wayland. Ordinary shortcuts go through Electron's `globalShortcut`, which only uses the Wayland portal when the app enables `GlobalShortcutsPortal` (`app.commandLine.appendSwitch('enable-features', 'GlobalShortcutsPortal')`), and the bundle doesn't. #38126 reports the voice chat hotkey not registering on Linux.

Possible approaches:

- **Shortcut and key release:** the `org.freedesktop.portal.GlobalShortcuts` portal has both `Activated` and `Deactivated` signals, so it could cover press and release. My GNOME 50.5 portal advertises both; #38126 reports the portal on KDE Plasma 6.7.4. Electron's `globalShortcut` only reports presses, so release would need the portal directly. A command-line or D-Bus toggle entry point would also let users bind the shortcut in their desktop's own keyboard settings.
- **Pasting:** XTest on X11. On Wayland, the RemoteDesktop portal's `NotifyKeyboardKeycode` (needs a RemoteDesktop session with keyboard access), or `ydotool` (needs its daemon and uinput access) or `wtype` (needs compositor virtual-keyboard support) where available. The existing paste-error recovery (overlay and clipboard retention) could be reused on Linux; #37443 covers silent insertion failures.
- **Toggle without key release:** a single-press start/stop toggle would avoid the current dependence on release events (see #46392).

### Additional information

Related: #38126 (Linux voice chat hotkey doesn't register), #46392 (single-press dictation hotkey), #37443 (keep the transcript when pasting fails).

items.title: Feature request: context-aware continuation actions + explicit interrupt control in ChatGPT Voice

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

items.body:
## Summary

ChatGPT should support two lightweight interaction controls for conversational flows where the user's intent is already obvious:

1. **Context-aware continuation actions** such as `Next`, `Continue`, `Next treasure`, `Show another`, or `Next step` when the assistant already knows the likely follow-up from the current conversation.
2. An explicit **Interrupt** control in ChatGPT Voice so the user can immediately stop the assistant's current spoken response without ending the Voice session.

These solve two opposite but related forms of friction: repeatedly having to say/type a trivial continuation token, and having no direct one-tap way to stop a spoken answer when the user wants to steer the conversation immediately.

## Part 1: Context-aware continuation action

This is not a request for a permanent generic `Next` button and not a request for automatic continuation. The assistant should infer when a short follow-up is semantically obvious from the conversation and offer that follow-up as a one-tap action.

Examples:

- `Next`
- `Continue`
- `Next treasure`
- `Show another`
- `Next step`
- `Keep going`

The label should be generated from the current conversation rather than hard-coded globally.

### Motivating example

In the observed ChatGPT conversation, the assistant explicitly ended with:

> Give me a “next treasure” whenever you want and I’ll bring exactly one excellent thing...

The user then had to manually send `Next` to obtain the already-defined next item.

At that point the conversational state is unambiguous: the model already knows what `Next` means, what content should follow, and that the user is expected to trigger it. Requiring the user to repeatedly type or say the same continuation token adds friction without adding information.

### Requested behavior

When the model has established a repeatable or sequential interaction and can identify a high-confidence next action, ChatGPT may return an optional structured suggested action alongside the response.

Example conceptual payload:

```text
label: "Next treasure"
action: send_followup
message: "Next treasure"
```

The client can render this as a compact button/chip below the assistant response or near the composer.

Tapping it should be equivalent to the user explicitly sending that follow-up message in the same conversation. It should create a normal user turn, preserve conversation history, and remain visible/auditable as user-initiated input.

### Useful Chat cases

- stories delivered one section at a time;
- recommendation discovery where the user asks for one item at a time;
- step-by-step tutoring;
- quizzes / flashcards;
- sequential troubleshooting;
- guided setup flows;
- repeated exploration such as `show another`, `next example`, or `continue`;
- any assistant response that explicitly asks the user for a short continuation token whose meaning is already fully determined by context.

The suggestion should disappear or change when the context changes. It should not survive blindly across unrelated turns.

## Part 2: Explicit Interrupt button in Voice

ChatGPT Voice should expose a clearly visible **Interrupt** / **Stop speaking** control while the assistant is actively talking.

The purpose is not to end Voice Mode. It should stop only the assistant's current spoken response and immediately return control to the user so they can speak or choose another action.

### Expected interaction

While the assistant is speaking:

1. A visible `Interrupt` / stop-speaking control is available.
2. Tapping it immediately halts audio playback/generation for the current response.
3. The Voice session remains open.
4. The microphone/input state becomes ready for the user to continue or redirect.
5. The interruption is reflected cleanly in conversation state so the next user turn starts from the actually heard/accepted boundary rather than pretending the entire spoken response completed normally.

### Why this matters

Voice conversations are more fluid than text. Users frequently realize mid-answer that:

- the assistant misunderstood the question;
- enough information has already been heard;
- they want to correct one detail immediately;
- they want to jump to the next item;
- they want to stop a long explanation without leaving Voice Mode.

Relying only on spoken barge-in can be unreliable in noisy environments, ambiguous when audio is playing, or harder for users with speech/accessibility constraints. A deterministic visual interrupt control gives the user an explicit escape hatch.

This should be distinct from:

- **End Voice session**: exits Voice Mode entirely.
- **Pause**: temporarily pauses playback but expects resumption.
- **Mute microphone**: controls user input, not assistant output.

The requested action is specifically: **terminate the current assistant utterance, keep the Voice session alive, and hand control back to the user immediately.**

## Voice + continuation together

The two controls work naturally together:

- while waiting for the user after a completed turn, Voice can show a context-aware action such as `Next treasure`;
- while the assistant is speaking, Voice can show an explicit `Interrupt` control;
- after interruption, the user can immediately speak a correction or tap the relevant next action.

This would make Voice feel much more like a controllable live conversation rather than a sequence of long audio blocks.

## Important product constraints

1. **User remains in control.** Do not auto-send or auto-continue without a tap/voice confirmation.
2. **Context-aware, not generic.** A permanent `Next` button would be wrong. Offer continuation only when the conversation establishes a clear continuation contract.
3. **Same semantics as a real user turn.** Tapping a continuation action should submit an ordinary follow-up message, not create a hidden execution path.
4. **Auditable.** Suggested-action taps and interruptions should map cleanly to visible conversation state.
5. **Multiple actions only when genuinely useful.** Prefer one strong continuation action over a row of speculative suggestions.
6. **No stale actions.** Suggestions should be invalidated when the thread state, pending question, tool state, or topic changes.
7. **Interrupt must be immediate.** It should stop the current assistant utterance without requiring the user to exit Voice Mode.
8. **Works across modalities.** Chat and Voice should share the same continuation semantics even if the visual treatment differs.

## Why this is different from generic suggested replies

The strongest continuation use case is not arbitrary next-message prediction. It is a **continuation contract already created by the assistant and accepted by the user**.

For example, after `I’ll give you exactly one item each time you say next`, the next-action semantics are already encoded in the conversation. The product can remove repetitive input while preserving explicit user control.

The interrupt control is the complementary mechanism for the opposite situation: when the user wants to stop the current output immediately and take back the floor.

## Possible implementation shape

Without assuming the current internal architecture, continuation actions could separate:

- `label`: concise UI copy shown to the user;
- `message`: the actual user follow-up to submit;
- optional `intent/type`: e.g. `continue_sequence`, `show_another`, `next_step`;
- lifecycle/validity tied to the assistant turn that proposed it.

Voice could expose a separate local/session control such as:

```text
action: interrupt_current_response
scope: current_voice_turn
preserve_session: true
```

The model should not need to invent client-specific UI markup. Structured action semantics could be rendered appropriately by Android, iOS, web, desktop, and Voice.

## Acceptance criteria

### Continuation flow

1. Assistant says it will provide one recommendation each time the user says `next`.
2. Assistant response includes a context-aware `Next` or more specific continuation action.
3. User taps the action.
4. The client submits a normal follow-up turn with the intended message.
5. The assistant provides the next item.
6. The next action is regenerated for the new state.
7. If the user instead changes topic, the stale action is removed.
8. Equivalent flow works in Voice with an appropriate tappable control.

### Voice interrupt flow

1. Start ChatGPT Voice and ask a question that produces a long spoken answer.
2. While the assistant is speaking, tap `Interrupt` / stop-speaking.
3. Audio stops immediately.
4. Voice Mode remains open.
5. The user can speak or tap another action immediately.
6. The next turn does not require waiting for the abandoned response to finish.
7. The conversation state reflects that the assistant response was interrupted rather than fully completed from the user's perspective.

## Environment / observed surface

- App: ChatGPT for Android **beta**
- App version: **1.2026.272**
- Android app build: **2627220**
- Device: **realme 9 Pro 5G (RMX3471)**
- OS: **Android 14**
- Surface: ordinary **ChatGPT Chat**; request also applies to **ChatGPT Voice**
- Observed: **2026-10-04**

A screenshot is available showing the user manually sending `Next` immediately after an assistant response that had already defined what `next` would mean.

## Duplicate review

I searched the public `openai/codex` tracker for suggested-reply / continuation / next-action button requests and did not find an issue matching this specific context-aware continuation contract across Chat and Voice. The Voice interrupt request is included here because it is part of the same lightweight conversational-control problem: one tap to either continue the already-understood flow or immediately take the floor back.

items.body:
## Summary

Android Codex Remote's `@` picker appears to have a plugin-metadata rendering/resolution failure.

The plugin entries themselves are present, but some are not rendered with their resolved presentation metadata. Two concrete symptoms are visible in the same picker:

1. **Icon resolution fails**: multiple unrelated plugins render with the same generic chain/link-style icon instead of their plugin-specific icon.
2. **Display-name resolution fails**: at least one plugin is shown using an internal/raw identifier such as `@dev-6ac098cdf18881918a738352224...` instead of the human-readable plugin name (`MegasMoves` / the configured display name).

This is not a request for Android Remote to copy another surface's layout. Different mobile/desktop layouts are fine. The bug is that Android Remote is exposing fallback/internal metadata instead of the resolved plugin presentation fields.

## Observed example

In the Android Remote `@` picker:

- normal entries such as `@sales` and `@sites` are listed,
- several entries share the same generic link icon,
- the MegasMoves plugin is displayed as a truncated internal developer/plugin ID beginning with `@dev-6ac098cdf...`, even though the product has a human-readable plugin name.

The subtitle for that same raw-ID entry still contains the plugin description (`Operate the embedded Megas MCP ...`), which suggests the plugin itself is known to the client and that only part of the presentation metadata is falling back or not being resolved.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Open the ChatGPT Android **beta** app.
2. Enter Codex Remote for a connected desktop host with multiple plugins available, including a developer/custom plugin.
3. Type `@` in the composer.
4. Scroll through the plugin/mention results.
5. Observe the presentation metadata for plugin rows.

## Expected behavior

For every plugin result, the Android Remote mention picker should render the resolved user-facing metadata supplied for that plugin, including:

- human-readable display name / mention label,
- plugin-specific icon,
- description/subtitle where available.

Internal plugin IDs should not be shown as the primary user-facing label unless no display name exists and that fallback is explicitly intended.

## Actual behavior

Some plugin rows fall back to incomplete/internal metadata:

- generic repeated link icons are used instead of plugin-specific icons,
- a raw internal `dev-...` plugin identifier is exposed as the mention label instead of the human-readable plugin name.

## Engineering hypothesis / area to inspect

Without asserting the root cause, this looks more like a **presentation-metadata hydration / normalization / fallback-path issue** than a plugin availability problem.

Useful places to inspect may include:

- the metadata object sent to the Android Remote mention picker for remote-installed/developer plugins,
- mapping from plugin ID -> display name / mention name / icon asset,
- whether Remote is receiving only the raw registry identifier while another metadata source contains the resolved branding,
- fallback ordering when icon/name fields are absent or late-loaded,
- whether developer/custom plugins take a different serialization path from bundled/curated plugins.

A strong regression test would render a mixed picker containing bundled, curated, and developer/custom plugins and assert that no internal `dev-*` ID is shown when a display name exists, and that distinct configured icons remain distinct.

## Environment

- App: ChatGPT for Android **beta**

- Device: **realme 9 Pro 5G (RMX3471)**
- OS: **Android 14**

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

items.body:
### What version of Codex is running?
0.160.0 (also read at commit 687a119)

### What happened?
With a custom model provider that has its own `auth` command and sends `x-openai-actor-authorization`, Codex offers the `image_gen` tool. If a ChatGPT Free-plan login is also saved on the machine, the tool is gone, although the turn never uses that login.

### Steps to reproduce
1. Configure a custom provider in `config.toml` with `auth.command` and an `x-openai-actor-authorization` HTTP header.
2. With no saved login, run a turn that asks for an image. `image_gen` is offered and the image is made.
3. Run `codex login` with a Free-plan ChatGPT account. Do not change the provider.
4. Run the same turn. `image_gen` is not in the tool list.

With a Plus-plan login in step 3, the tool stays.

### Root cause
`image_generation_available` (`codex-rs/core/src/tools/spec_plan.rs:727`) returns false on `account_plan_type() == Some(PlanType::Free)` before it reads the provider. It reads the plan from the session auth manager (`core/src/session/turn_context.rs:1239`), which holds the saved ChatGPT login. The provider has its own auth manager (`model-provider/src/auth.rs:187`, `external_bearer_only`), and that is the one used for the request.

### Expected
The Free-plan check applies only when the turn uses the ChatGPT login, for example when `provider.requires_openai_auth` is true. A provider with its own auth, or one that sends the actor header, is not limited by the plan of a login it does not use.

### Workaround
`-c cli_auth_credentials_store="ephemeral"` hides the saved login and brings the tool back, at the cost of the login for that launch.
